drug_class: Selective norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor (SNRI) — non-stimulant ADHD medication
purpose: Atomoxetine is used to treat Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) in children, teenagers, and adults. It helps improve focus, reduce impulsiveness, and control hyperactivity. Unlike many ADHD medications, it is not a stimulant, so it is a good option for people who cannot take stimulant medicines.
how_it_works: Your brain uses a chemical called norepinephrine to help with attention and self-control. Atomoxetine works by keeping more of this chemical available in the brain for longer. This helps the parts of your brain that manage focus and behavior work better throughout the day.
common_side_effects: Some common side effects include upset stomach, nausea, decreased appetite, dry mouth, dizziness, tiredness, and trouble sleeping. Some people may notice a slight increase in heart rate or blood pressure. These effects are often mild and may improve after the first few weeks of taking the medication.
warnings: This medication carries a warning about a small risk of suicidal thoughts, especially in children and teenagers — contact your doctor right away if you notice mood changes or unusual thoughts. It can also rarely cause liver problems, so tell your doctor if you notice yellowing of the skin or eyes, dark urine, or stomach pain. Do not take it if you have taken an MAO inhibitor (like phenelzine) in the last 14 days, as this can cause a dangerous reaction. Tell your doctor about any heart conditions before starting this medicine.
typical_dosing: For children and teens weighing up to 70 kg (about 154 lbs), the usual starting dose is about 0.5 mg per kg of body weight per day, which may be increased after a week or two. For adults and larger patients, the typical starting dose is 40 mg per day, which may be increased to 80–100 mg per day. It can be taken once in the morning or split into two doses (morning and late afternoon). It takes several weeks to feel the full benefit, so be patient and do not stop without talking to your doctor.
